title: Work, Moments and Springs
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Work, Moments and Springs Worksheets (Levers, Hooke's Law)
standard_text: Forces as pushes or pulls, arising from the interaction between two objects; using force arrows in diagrams; moment as the turning effect of a force; forces: associated with deforming objects; stretching and squashing – springs; with rubbing and friction between surfaces; forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's Law as a special case; work done and energy changes on deformation; simple machines give bigger force but at the expense of smaller movement (and vice versa): product of force and displacement unchanged.
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on work done, moments, balancing see-saws, levers and simple machines, and stretching springs with Hooke's law. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: moment = force × distance from the pivot
key_sub: Work done = force × distance; extension is proportional to force.
body_html:
How to think about it

Forces can do work, turn things and stretch things.

  • work done (J) = force (N) × distance moved (m).
  • moment (N m) = force (N) × distance from the pivot (m). Balanced: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments.
  • A spring's extension is proportional to the force (Hooke's law), up to its limit.
Example

50 N pushes 4 m. Work?

50 × 4

Answer: 200 J

Example

20 N at 0.5 m from a pivot. Moment?

20 × 0.5

Answer: 10 N m

Common mistakes

  • Adding force and distance instead of multiplying.
  • Thinking the heavier person sits further from the pivot.
  • Mixing up length and extension.

faq.q: How do you calculate work done?
faq.a: Multiply the force by the distance moved in the direction of the force: work done = force × distance. The unit is the joule.

faq.q: How do you balance a see-saw?
faq.a: The clockwise moment must equal the anticlockwise moment. A lighter person must sit further from the pivot than a heavier one.
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force on it, as long as it is not stretched past its limit of proportionality.
